Washington is bucking almost every historic precedent. Teams with rosters this young have by and large been very, very bad.

Even when accounting for the fact the WNBA has diluted the talent pool a bit through expansion, putting together a winning record when only three players on the roster have more than one year of service time is incredible.

For right now, the Mystics are playing with house money because they're ahead of schedule in their rebuild. Winning a series would be nice, but simply having Citron, Iriafen, Betts and McMahon taste playoff basketball is important in its own right.
The postseason could also be instructive to the coaching staff and front office toward how to continue building around Citron and Iriafen.

articles.title: 30 Overreactions to the 2026 NBA Offseason
articles.summary: Every NBA offseason has a different theme to it.
articles.body:
Every NBA offseason has a different theme to it.

This year's was a fun one: There was never a dull moment.

Just when you thought you might have all the splashes accounted for, something else would make a splash and send the basketball world into another reshuffling.

With action like this, imaginations are running wild about what all of this activity (or, in certain cases, inactivity) might mean for the short- and long-term future.

We can only guesstimate how things will go, which leads to a lot of overreactions. Like, say, one for all 30 teams.

Overreaction: The NBA has a new best defense.

The Hawks had last season's 10th-best defense ( fifth-best after Trae Young played his final game in Atlanta). This summer, they added 2024-25 All-Defensive first-teamer Lu Dort and fellow former shape-shifting member of the Oklahoma City Thunder Aaron Wiggins.

Couple them with what was already a wealth of defensive talent, and you're now looking at the league's stingiest defense, right?

Maybe , but let's see it in action before making such a definitive declaration. The Hawks should be all kinds of disruptive on defense. Sure, the Thunder still have a pretty terrific collection of stoppers, the San Antonio Spurs have that 7-foot-something alien everyone keeps talking about, and the Detroit Pistons employ a host of long-limbed, physical defenders.

The Hawks look poised to rank among the league's best defenses, but crowning them No. 1 already is an unnecessary rush to judgment.

The Celtics shattered expectations with a 56-win effort last season, and then promptly traded away the MVP candidate spawned during the campaign (Jaylen Brown, who landed sixth in MVP voting and second team All-NBA) for pennies on the dollar. Jayson Tatum is suddenly without a co-star, and that probably means Boston is out of the title race—for now.

The Celtics lack the high-end star power to contend for the crown right now, but they might only be an upgrade or two to rejoining the heavyweight contender ranks.

And since they have some wiggle room—a handful of first-round picks to throw around, some monster contracts coming off the books over the next few summers—they just might make those additions before the 28-year-old Tatum ages out of his prime.

Overreaction: They'll have the NBA's best backcourt in five years or less.

Those who kept an eye on Brooklyn's summer league squads surely had a chance to overindulge on optimism surrounding this year's No. 6 pick Mikel Brown Jr. and last year's No. 8 pick Egor Dëmin.

Between the former's flashy play style and the latter's ability to utilize his added muscle, they raised expectations by the minute and even gained a shared nickname along the way.

Excitement is fine (and fully warranted), but it still needs to stay within reason. This guard group has an undeniable chance to be awesome, but it remains only a possibility. Dëmin averaged 10.3 points on 39.9 percent shooting as a rookie, and Brown shot 41 percent during his lone season of college ball.

Their individual paths to stardom are steep.

Overreaction: They will regret dismantling their core.

The Hornets had a wholly ridiculous January to April stretch in which they went 33-16 with the league's best net rating ( plus-10.5 ). But they just snatched the wind from their own sails by jettisoning two key contributors (LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges) in offseason trades.

And guess what? It was the right call. Ball, a walking injury risk with less than stellar play-style reviews , brought back Naz Reid, an unprotected first-round pick, three first-round swaps and three second-round picks.

Bridges, a volume scorer with a lot of hollow stats, somehow delivered an unprotected future first. The value was impossible to pass up, and they can now grow a more accommodating and sustainable core around cornerstones Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller.

Overreaction: They blew their cap space on nothing.

This was supposed to be a transformational summer for the Bulls, and in certain ways, it was. Their front office got an overdue overhaul, and the draft lottery delivered a pair of possible building blocks (No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson and No. 15 pick Dailyn Swain). But the gobs of cap space they possessed wound up delivering only Nic Claxton, Norman Powell and Zach Collins (and hopes of a late Bennedict Mathurin addition). Yikes, right?

Well, sort of, but they had to find someone to man the middle and landed a perfectly suitable solution with the 27-year-old Claxton. And they needed someone to help pick up the scoring slack, and Powell, a 21-plus-point scorer the past two seasons, should be up to that challenge. Neither may stick around Chicago long, but that's probably the point—lean on the vets now as their prospects find their footing and then flip those players for more long-term assets when the youth is ready to take over.

Overreaction: They finally cracked the code at small forward.

Ever since Cleveland brought Donovan Mitchell to town, this organization has chased one possible solution at small forward after the next. Could that carousel finally stop spinning? That's surely the hope after this front office burned its remaining draft assets to be crowned surprise winners of the Peyton Watson sweepstakes.

This had to be encouraging, if only to see Cleveland do something in response to the many splashes made by fellow East elites. That said, it's not like Watson's arrival guarantees the Cavs finally have their missing piece at the 3. He is a stingy, disruptive defender, but his offense is very much a work in progress.

If he can't crank up the three-point volume while sustaining his newfound efficiency, it could be hard for this offense to breathe when he's slotting alongside Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen.

Overreaction: This roster makes no sense.

The Mavericks' roster reads like it's stuck between two eras—probably because it is.

Kyrie Irving leads a veteran core that was initially brought together to give Luka Dončić a championship chance. Meanwhile, a young nucleus is starting to take shape around 2025 top pick Cooper Flagg. This group is also light on ball-handlers and heavier than it needs to be with forwards.

And yet, this might somehow be the right spot for the Mavericks at the moment. They're still figuring things out with Flagg, like how he'll fare alongside an established star like Irving (who missed all of last season while rehabbing a torn ACL).

They're also in no rush to move veterans ( other than perhaps Klay Thompson), since they could try to compete with them first, knowing they'll always maintain trade value.

Overreaction: They're giving Nikola Jokić reasons to consider leaving.

Setting aside any sentimental attachments or the desire to complete a career with one franchise, what is the great argument for Jokić recommitting to Denver ? The Nuggets are still a really good team, but is greatness a legitimate possibility? They've won two total playoff series in the three seasons since their 2023 title run, and their already compromised defense now must find a way to proceed without Peyton Watson.

All of this feels ominous, yet none of it really matters unless Jokić decides it does. And so far, nothing has changed the notion that he plans to continue his career in Denver. ( Well, nothing other than the dreams of hopeful poachers .) The Nuggets should be careful about taking his presence for granted, but it hardly sounds like he is scanning for the exits.

Overreaction: Cade Cunningham's co-star isn't coming.

The rumor mill connected the Pistons to some fascinating scenarios this summer, but nothing major materialized. Labeling their offseason dud is a bit harsh—John Collins can pile up points, and Isaiah Joe's shooting scratches a big itch—but it's certainly disappointing when weighed against some of those initial expectations, especially when nothing has been figured out with Jalen Duren yet.

This all leaves Cunningham without the co-star he seemingly needs to make a real championship push. Detroit will have more chances, though. If the Pistons can't develop that player (maybe Duren or Ausar Thompson), they'll still have the assets needed to go pursue a needle-mover in a trade.

Overreaction: They failed Stephen Curry.

As shepherds of Curry's once-in-a-lifetime career, the Warriors have some responsibility for ensuring he has a chance to play for something of significance. So, when they're effectively running back a 45-loss roster for what will be his age-38 season, it sure feels like a franchise-wide failure.

Maybe history will remember it as such, but Golden State still has a chance to field a more formidable supporting cast around him. It'll just take some time to make that happen. The Warriors have draft capital to throw around and navigable paths toward big-time financial flexibility, plus a potential difference-maker on the mend in Jimmy Butler, so things aren't nearly as dire as they may initially appear.

After following consecutive 52-win campaigns with first-round exits, the Rockets appeared open for anything this summer. They gave potential trade partners the impression that Amen Thompson was their "only near untouchable," per Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko , suggesting their roster might look dramatically different for the 2026-27 season.

When considering the potential activity, this feels a lot closer to status quo. This is not, however, a stationary squad. Fred VanVleet is back, Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanović have joined the party and the young core has had another offseason of development. Splash-less summer or not, it's still a collective stock up for Space City.

Overreaction: A sleepy summer has them set up for disappointment.

Tyrese Haliburton has wondered aloud why the league isn't treating his return from a torn Achilles as a bigger deal. Clearly, expectations in the Circle City are enormous with the franchise floor general back and Ivica Zubac manning the middle.

You wonder whether expectations will be too high, though, given all that has changed in the East since Indiana booked that surprise trip to the 2025 NBA Finals.

When players like Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James and (presumably) Kawhi Leonard are moving around, that activity tends to overshadow the return of a small-market's star. But Haliburton might be onto something.

This offense hums when he's at the helm, and Zubac can be a stabilizer at center. The Pacers didn't need a busy summer to drum up excitement (at least internally) around their chances for the upcoming campaign.

Overreaction: Keaton Wagler was exposed in Summer League.

With the Clippers in the process of closing out the Kawhi Leonard chapter, Wagler, their No. 5 pick, is prominently positioned for whatever comes next. So, he had plenty of eyeballs on him at summer league, and he didn't exactly thrive under the spotlight. He was an inefficient scorer and an ineffective contributor in virtually every other category.

It was disappointing to see. It was also potentially meaningless. Las Vegas has a history of fooling the hoops world with mirages . And Wagler, who impacts the game more with feel than freakish physical tools, never figured to thrive in that environment. You'd still prefer to see him star at summer league, but overreacting to the fact he didn't is pointless.

Overreaction: They just pumped all of their assets into a Play-In roster.

The Lakers prioritized a new contract for Austin Reaves and finding an impact center this offseason. They managed to check both boxes, but they paid an exorbitant cost to do it: $184.8 million for Reaves, and then two first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps for the right to give Walker Kessler $129.5 million.

Luka Dončić at least seems on board with the moves , but there isn't an obvious way for L.A. to wiggle out of this should things run awry.

And maybe that's OK. Dončić plus a second scorer and shot-creator has proved an awful potent combo in the past. Dončić plus an impact center has typically delivered results, too. If L.A. works some developmental magic on the likes of Cameron Carr, Adou Thiero and Quentin Grimes, this roster could surprise sooner than later.

Overreaction: Cameron Boozer should've been the No. 1 pick.

Did anyone catch Boozer's run with the summer-league Grizzlies? You might still be cleaning up drool puddles if you did. He was any and everything he was billed to be: versatile, productive, efficient and absolutely impactful on winning.

So, should he be cemented on way-too-early re-draft boards now? Nope. The skills he showed in summer league were never questioned; any knocks were always tied to the fact he lagged behind both AJ Dybantsa and Darryn Peterson in terms of physical tools, which is clearly still the case. Boozer might already have the highest floor of the three, but teams holding the No. 1 pick are seeking more than safety.

Overreaction: Landing a whale unlocks immediate championship possibilities.

For years, the Heat waited for this very opportunity—not simply landing a superstar, but getting Giannis freakin' Antetokounmpo. And given how successful they'd managed to be in some of those superstar-less seasons, his addition has to make them an immediate factor in the championship chase, right?

Well, you never want to rule out anything involving a player this talented, but this roster has question marks all around the Antetokounmpo-Bam Adebayo combo (which has its own logistical concerns with spacing). Throw in the rising tides of a fully loaded East, and Miami isn't guaranteed a top-six seed, much less a legitimate shot at winning it all.

Overreaction: They botched the Giannis Antetokounmpo blockbuster.

By the time the Bucks got around to trading away Antetokounmpo, he was entrenched as the best player in franchise history. And through that lens, Milwaukee's return package—Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel'el Ware, Kasparas Jakučionis, three firsts, a swap and a second—might seem so underwhelming to make you think the Bucks really botched this.

They didn't. Or they didn't botch it this offseason, at least. Teams weren't beating that offer (especially if Milwaukee thinks the homegrown Herro is a keeper) for a 31-year-old with shooting limitations, contract uncertainty and some recent injury trouble. The Bucks just needed to rip this Band-Aid off sooner. Everyone outside of Milwaukee could see this coming and delaying the inevitable denied this club what could have been a truly ridiculous collection of incoming assets.

Overreaction: Anthony Edwards has a championship chance now.

The Wolves needed more consistent offensive support for Edwards and just found it in LaMelo Ball, a nightly 20-point, 10-assist threat with deep shooting range, two-steps-ahead passing vision and gobs of creativity. This was someone whom Minnesota's decision-makers "had long believed was the ideal backcourt running mate for Anthony Edwards," per The Athletic's Jon Krawczynski .

The Wolves' working theory is a fun one. It's also risky as heck. Minnesota effectively drained its asset pool and changed identities for an offense-leaning (or offense-only) player who owns a career 41.8 field-goal percentage and has reached the playoffs exactly zero times. Oh, and he has played fewer than 52 games in four of his six seasons. It would be objectively awesome if this works, but the list of reasons to believe it won't is not a short one.

Overreaction: They missed their window to reset.

Sellers were in top demand this offseason as there weren't enough impact players to satiate the many buyers. Shouldn't the Pelicans have used that to their advantage? Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones should've had rich markets, and Zion Williamson might've even been movable after making 60-plus appearances for the second time in the last three seasons.

For whatever reason, though, the stars never aligned on a swap. Maybe that was a major misfire by New Orleans, but executive vice president of basketball operations Joe Dumars told NOLA.com's Rod Walker the inactivity was "not from a lack of effort or us deciding we didn't want to do anything." The Pelicans seemingly just didn't back down from the prices they set, and there's a chance their patience will be rewarded the next time trade season gets rolling.

Overreaction: Their roster won't be the same without Mitchell Robinson.

It could be ages before the Knicks wind up with a player as big and bouncy as Robinson. The 7-foot rim-runner may not have been the most durable player around, but he always made his presence felt in small doses. Despite often operating opposite New York's stacked starting lineup, Robinson managed to post a plus-2.6 net differential .

New York will miss Robinson's paint presence and anti-gravity ups, but not in a this-club-can't-repeat kind of way. The Knicks gave him fewer than 20 minutes in the regular season and trimmed that to less than 14 in the playoffs, so they're only filling a niche role. And Andre Drummond should be a serviceable replacement, especially on a minimum contract.

Overreaction: Dynasties are impossible in the NBA's economic environment.

The Thunder won 132 regular-season games and six playoff series over the past two seasons. They traded away three rotation regulars over the offseason, and not to accommodate newcomers but rather to make the budget more manageable. Such is life under this collective bargaining agreement.

Or is it? Because these maneuvers weren't apron-related. As The Athletic's Fred Katz relayed, "In the league's third-smallest market, owner Clay Bennett is sticking to a budget."

Other organizations won't give themselves the same restrictions, meaning their budgets could certainly stretch farther than this, especially if doing so meant keeping a potential dynasty together.

Overreaction: They're denying the reality of their wing tandem.

The Magic just played their fourth season with both Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner on the wing. They even propped up that pairing with a bold (and budget-busting) trade for Desmond Bane. Yet, they're still awaiting the first playoff series win of the Banchero-Wagner era. Perhaps because this twosome just doesn't work.

But the Magic are right for thinking it's too soon to make that call. A coaching change could help better align the puzzle pieces. And there are still ways to tweak this core without demolishing the foundation. Teams rarely improve by trading their best players away.

Overreaction: This offense has too many mouths to feed.

Every time a superteam is spawned, the same concern rises shortly thereafter: There's only one basketball to go around . As if that reality doesn't exist for every other team in the Association.

Will it be simple to satisfy all four of LeBron James, Jaylen Brown, Tyrese Maxey and Joel Embiid? Nope—but that's a problem that just about every other franchise would love to try tackling.

"Talking to (head coach Nick Nurse), he's excited. It's just like a kid in a candy store," Sixers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey told reporters . "He's like, 'How are we going to put this thing together and see if it works?'"

When that one basketball goes around, it will often find its way to either a former MVP or a current All-NBA honoree. If Philly can strike the right balance, this offense should be silly.

Overreaction: Devin Booker still has no help.

The Suns stripped themselves of a Booker co-star when they traded Kevin Durant last offseason. At this rate, it doesn't feel like they're even searching for one. When they're adding talent, it's of the role-playing variety: Miles Bridges as a scoring forward, Luke Kennard as a net-shredder, Koa Peat as a forceful dot-connector.

Maybe this all means the whole outpaces the sum of the parts again. Phoenix overpaid for Bridges, but it did have a void to fill at power forward. It signed a lot of sensible contracts, which should remain movable if a direction change is needed. And things aren't even helpless on the co-star front, as big developmental leaps could still be in front of Jalen Green and Khaman Maluach, and the regression that was supposed to hit Dillon Brooks in the playoffs never came close to materializing.

The Blazers saw an offer they couldn't refuse. That's the only rationale that makes sense behind their summer swap of Jerami Grant and Kris Murray for Ja Morant. And honestly, that reasoning is sound. It's sort of a no-risk, all-reward wager on a two-time All-Star who just turned 27. In a vacuum, there's a lot to love.

Basketball teams don't play in a vacuum, though, and this is one situation where the old there's only one ball thing feels legitimately worrisome. How does a roster simultaneously squeeze the most out of Morant, Damian Lillard, Scoot Henderson and Jrue Holiday? And how does that guard group not totally torpedo the on-ball opportunities for All-Star swingman Deni Avdija? Even in a positionless league, there are too many cooks in this kitchen.

Overreaction: Darius Acuff Jr. is doomed.

Summer league was rough for Acuff. His scoring volume reached an acceptable level, but that was it for positives. His efficiency underwhelmed, his playmaking unraveled amid a sea of turnovers and his defense lived up to its unfavorable billing.

None of that necessarily matters, though. Acuff handled a heavy responsibility list as a teenager in a chaotic environment. Things going well may have been more surprising than these struggles.

As far as there are worries with Acuff, who won't turn 20 until November, they hinge more around his chances of germinating in what has been, shall we say, less than fruitful soil in Sacramento.

Overreaction: De'Aaron Fox has got to go.

The NBA Finals put the worst kind of spotlight onto Fox. He not only struggled in major moments, he also saw the player right behind him on the depth chart, last summer's No. 2 pick Dylan Harper, succeed in such a way that everyone wondered why he wasn't getting more minutes . The worst read on the situation painted Fox as a $221.7 million obstacle in San Antonio's path.

That's not at all how the Spurs see it, though. General manager Brian Wright expressed "the ultimate faith in De'Aaron," and The Athletic's Jared Weiss relayed that "multiple team and league sources said the Spurs still see Fox as a critical piece of the team's future." This is how San Antonio needs to handle this, since it has enough floor time and touches to get the best out of its three-headed monster in the backcourt, and it needs the on-court organization Fox offers.

Overreaction: Summer League proved Allen Graves was a steal.

Graves was a curiosity in college, a reserve on a mid-major with some of the best analytics around. Toronto snatched him up with this summer's 19th pick, and he immediately showcased his versatility on the summer circuit: 16.8 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 2.3 steals across four contests.

It was a proof-of-concept performance for everyone who saw him as a potential Swiss Army knife.

It was also maybe indicative of nothing for his future. His lack of athleticism could be a real challenge against actual NBA defenders, and his outside shooting still has to prove sustainable with a significant increase in volume.

This isn't to say Toronto fans should abandon hope. It's just a reminder that those hopes are nothing more than that at this stage.

Overreaction: Darryn Peterson isn't a playmaker.

Peterson's improvement as a playmaker in high school played a big part in his standing as a top 2026 draft prospect. Then, he went to Kansas and totaled exactly as many turnovers as assists (38 each) in 24 games. Next, he technically fared slightly better at Sacramento—26 assists against 24 turnovers in five outings.

This could be a cause for major concern, but it's too early to really raise that alarm. For one, he could star without a ton of passing production as an all-purpose shotmaker in a multi-distributor offense. Second, he showed advanced passing reads as a prep star, and he might just need better health and superior scoring help around him to get back into that bag.

After three straight seasons with 64-plus losses, the Wizards are putting their losing ways behind them. Washington has organically grown a compelling young core and then supplemented it with established stars (Trae Young, Anthony Davis) and the No. 1 pick in a highly celebrated draft (AJ Dybantsa).

The Wizards even brought back Khris Middleton and turned their attention toward DeMar DeRozan after a failed courtship of Russell Westbrook.

Clearly, Washington thinks it is ready to turn the corner. A bit of brake-pumping feels warranted. Young is a one-way contributor, Davis can't stay on the court (and isn't a lock to stick around) and this young nucleus has won nothing at this level.

The future is bright—there's no denying that—but Washington may not be out of the woods just yet.

They gave potential trade partners the impression that Amen Thompson was their "only near untouchable," per Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko , suggesting their roster might look dramatically different for the 2026-27 season.

When considering the potential activity, this feels a lot closer to status quo. This is not, however, a stationary squad. Fred VanVleet is back, Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanović have joined the party and the young core has had another offseason of development. Splash-less summer or not, it's still a collective stock up for Space City.
Overreaction: A sleepy summer has them set up for disappointment.

Tyrese Haliburton has wondered aloud why the league isn't treating his return from a torn Achilles as a bigger deal. Clearly, expectations in the Circle City are enormous with the franchise floor general back and Ivica Zubac manning the middle.
You wonder whether expectations will be too high, though, given all that has changed in the East since Indiana booked that surprise trip to the 2025 NBA Finals.

When players like Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James and (presumably) Kawhi Leonard are moving around, that activity tends to overshadow the return of a small-market's star. But Haliburton might be onto something.

This offense hums when he's at the helm, and Zubac can be a stabilizer at center. The Pacers didn't need a busy summer to drum up excitement (at least internally) around their chances for the upcoming campaign.
Overreaction: Keaton Wagler was exposed in Summer League.

With the Clippers in the process of closing out the Kawhi Leonard chapter, Wagler, their No. 5 pick, is prominently positioned for whatever comes next. So, he had plenty of eyeballs on him at summer league, and he didn't exactly thrive under the spotlight. He was an inefficient scorer and an ineffective contributor in virtually every other category.

It was disappointing to see. It was also potentially meaningless. Las Vegas has a history of fooling the hoops world with mirages . And Wagler, who impacts the game more with feel than freakish physical tools, never figured to thrive in that environment. You'd still prefer to see him star at summer league, but overreacting to the fact he didn't is pointless.
Overreaction: They just pumped all of their assets into a Play-In roster.

The Lakers prioritized a new contract for Austin Reaves and finding an impact center this offseason. They managed to check both boxes, but they paid an exorbitant cost to do it: $184.8 million for Reaves, and then two first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps for the right to give Walker Kessler $129.5 million.
Luka Dončić at least seems on board with the moves , but there isn't an obvious way for L.A. to wiggle out of this should things run awry.

And maybe that's OK. Dončić plus a second scorer and shot-creator has proved an awful potent combo in the past. Dončić plus an impact center has typically delivered results, too. If L.A. works some developmental magic on the likes of Cameron Carr, Adou Thiero and Quentin Grimes, this roster could surprise sooner than later.
Overreaction: Cameron Boozer should've been the No. 1 pick.

Did anyone catch Boozer's run with the summer-league Grizzlies? You might still be cleaning up drool puddles if you did. He was any and everything he was billed to be: versatile, productive, efficient and absolutely impactful on winning.

So, should he be cemented on way-too-early re-draft boards now? Nope. The skills he showed in summer league were never questioned; any knocks were always tied to the fact he lagged behind both AJ Dybantsa and Darryn Peterson in terms of physical tools, which is clearly still the case. Boozer might already have the highest floor of the three, but teams holding the No. 1 pick are seeking more than safety.
Overreaction: Landing a whale unlocks immediate championship possibilities.

For years, the Heat waited for this very opportunity—not simply landing a superstar, but getting Giannis freakin' Antetokounmpo. And given how successful they'd managed to be in some of those superstar-less seasons, his addition has to make them an immediate factor in the championship chase, right?

Well, you never want to rule out anything involving a player this talented, but this roster has question marks all around the Antetokounmpo-Bam Adebayo combo (which has its own logistical concerns with spacing). Throw in the rising tides of a fully loaded East, and Miami isn't guaranteed a top-six seed, much less a legitimate shot at winning it all.
Overreaction: They botched the Giannis Antetokounmpo blockbuster.

By the time the Bucks got around to trading away Antetokounmpo, he was entrenched as the best player in franchise history. And through that lens, Milwaukee's return package—Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel'el Ware, Kasparas Jakučionis, three firsts, a swap and a second—might seem so underwhelming to make you think the Bucks really botched this.

They didn't. Or they didn't botch it this offseason, at least. Teams weren't beating that offer (especially if Milwaukee thinks the homegrown Herro is a keeper) for a 31-year-old with shooting limitations, contract uncertainty and some recent injury trouble. The Bucks just needed to rip this Band-Aid off sooner. Everyone outside of Milwaukee could see this coming and delaying the inevitable denied this club what could have been a truly ridiculous collection of incoming assets.
Overreaction: Anthony Edwards has a championship chance now.

The Wolves needed more consistent offensive support for Edwards and just found it in LaMelo Ball, a nightly 20-point, 10-assist threat with deep shooting range, two-steps-ahead passing vision and gobs of creativity. This was someone whom Minnesota's decision-makers "had long believed was the ideal backcourt running mate for Anthony Edwards," per The Athletic's Jon Krawczynski .

The Wolves' working theory is a fun one. It's also risky as heck. Minnesota effectively drained its asset pool and changed identities for an offense-leaning (or offense-only) player who owns a career 41.8 field-goal percentage and has reached the playoffs exactly zero times. Oh, and he has played fewer than 52 games in four of his six seasons. It would be objectively awesome if this works, but the list of reasons to believe it won't is not a short one.
Overreaction: They missed their window to reset.

Sellers were in top demand this offseason as there weren't enough impact players to satiate the many buyers. Shouldn't the Pelicans have used that to their advantage? Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones should've had rich markets, and Zion Williamson might've even been movable after making 60-plus appearances for the second time in the last three seasons.

For whatever reason, though, the stars never aligned on a swap. Maybe that was a major misfire by New Orleans, but executive vice president of basketball operations Joe Dumars told NOLA.com's Rod Walker the inactivity was "not from a lack of effort or us deciding we didn't want to do anything." The Pelicans seemingly just didn't back down from the prices they set, and there's a chance their patience will be rewarded the next time trade season gets rolling.
Overreaction: Their roster won't be the same without Mitchell Robinson.

It could be ages before the Knicks wind up with a player as big and bouncy as Robinson. The 7-foot rim-runner may not have been the most durable player around, but he always made his presence felt in small doses. Despite often operating opposite New York's stacked starting lineup, Robinson managed to post a plus-2.6 net differential .

New York will miss Robinson's paint presence and anti-gravity ups, but not in a this-club-can't-repeat kind of way. The Knicks gave him fewer than 20 minutes in the regular season and trimmed that to less than 14 in the playoffs, so they're only filling a niche role. And Andre Drummond should be a serviceable replacement, especially on a minimum contract.
Overreaction: Dynasties are impossible in the NBA's economic environment.

The Thunder won 132 regular-season games and six playoff series over the past two seasons. They traded away three rotation regulars over the offseason, and not to accommodate newcomers but rather to make the budget more manageable. Such is life under this collective bargaining agreement.
Or is it? Because these maneuvers weren't apron-related. As The Athletic's Fred Katz relayed, "In the league's third-smallest market, owner Clay Bennett is sticking to a budget."
Other organizations won't give themselves the same restrictions, meaning their budgets could certainly stretch farther than this, especially if doing so meant keeping a potential dynasty together.
Overreaction: They're denying the reality of their wing tandem.

The Magic just played their fourth season with both Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner on the wing. They even propped up that pairing with a bold (and budget-busting) trade for Desmond Bane. Yet, they're still awaiting the first playoff series win of the Banchero-Wagner era. Perhaps because this twosome just doesn't work.

But the Magic are right for thinking it's too soon to make that call. A coaching change could help better align the puzzle pieces. And there are still ways to tweak this core without demolishing the foundation. Teams rarely improve by trading their best players away.
Overreaction: This offense has too many mouths to feed.
Every time a superteam is spawned, the same concern rises shortly thereafter: There's only one basketball to go around . As if that reality doesn't exist for every other team in the Association.
Will it be simple to satisfy all four of LeBron James, Jaylen Brown, Tyrese Maxey and Joel Embiid? Nope—but that's a problem that just about every other franchise would love to try tackling.

"Talking to (head coach Nick Nurse), he's excited. It's just like a kid in a candy store," Sixers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey told reporters . "He's like, 'How are we going to put this thing together and see if it works?'"
When that one basketball goes around, it will often find its way to either a former MVP or a current All-NBA honoree. If Philly can strike the right balance, this offense should be silly.
Overreaction: Devin Booker still has no help.

The Suns stripped themselves of a Booker co-star when they traded Kevin Durant last offseason. At this rate, it doesn't feel like they're even searching for one. When they're adding talent, it's of the role-playing variety: Miles Bridges as a scoring forward, Luke Kennard as a net-shredder, Koa Peat as a forceful dot-connector.

Maybe this all means the whole outpaces the sum of the parts again. Phoenix overpaid for Bridges, but it did have a void to fill at power forward. It signed a lot of sensible contracts, which should remain movable if a direction change is needed. And things aren't even helpless on the co-star front, as big developmental leaps could still be in front of Jalen Green and Khaman Maluach, and the regression that was supposed to hit Dillon Brooks in the playoffs never came close to materializing.

The Blazers saw an offer they couldn't refuse. That's the only rationale that makes sense behind their summer swap of Jerami Grant and Kris Murray for Ja Morant. And honestly, that reasoning is sound. It's sort of a no-risk, all-reward wager on a two-time All-Star who just turned 27. In a vacuum, there's a lot to love.

Basketball teams don't play in a vacuum, though, and this is one situation where the old there's only one ball thing feels legitimately worrisome. How does a roster simultaneously squeeze the most out of Morant, Damian Lillard, Scoot Henderson and Jrue Holiday? And how does that guard group not totally torpedo the on-ball opportunities for All-Star swingman Deni Avdija? Even in a positionless league, there are too many cooks in this kitchen.
Overreaction: Darius Acuff Jr. is doomed.

Summer league was rough for Acuff. His scoring volume reached an acceptable level, but that was it for positives. His efficiency underwhelmed, his playmaking unraveled amid a sea of turnovers and his defense lived up to its unfavorable billing.
None of that necessarily matters, though. Acuff handled a heavy responsibility list as a teenager in a chaotic environment. Things going well may have been more surprising than these struggles.
As far as there are worries with Acuff, who won't turn 20 until November, they hinge more around his chances of germinating in what has been, shall we say, less than fruitful soil in Sacramento.
Overreaction: De'Aaron Fox has got to go.

The NBA Finals put the worst kind of spotlight onto Fox. He not only struggled in major moments, he also saw the player right behind him on the depth chart, last summer's No. 2 pick Dylan Harper, succeed in such a way that everyone wondered why he wasn't getting more minutes . The worst read on the situation painted Fox as a $221.7 million obstacle in San Antonio's path.

That's not at all how the Spurs see it, though. General manager Brian Wright expressed "the ultimate faith in De'Aaron," and The Athletic's Jared Weiss relayed that "multiple team and league sources said the Spurs still see Fox as a critical piece of the team's future." This is how San Antonio needs to handle this, since it has enough floor time and touches to get the best out of its three-headed monster in the backcourt, and it needs the on-court organization Fox offers.
Overreaction: Summer League proved Allen Graves was a steal.

Graves was a curiosity in college, a reserve on a mid-major with some of the best analytics around. Toronto snatched him up with this summer's 19th pick, and he immediately showcased his versatility on the summer circuit: 16.8 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 2.3 steals across four contests.
It was a proof-of-concept performance for everyone who saw him as a potential Swiss Army knife.

It was also maybe indicative of nothing for his future. His lack of athleticism could be a real challenge against actual NBA defenders, and his outside shooting still has to prove sustainable with a significant increase in volume.
This isn't to say Toronto fans should abandon hope. It's just a reminder that those hopes are nothing more than that at this stage.
Overreaction: Darryn Peterson isn't a playmaker.

Peterson's improvement as a playmaker in high school played a big part in his standing as a top 2026 draft prospect. Then, he went to Kansas and totaled exactly as many turnovers as assists (38 each) in 24 games. Next, he technically fared slightly better at Sacramento—26 assists against 24 turnovers in five outings.

This could be a cause for major concern, but it's too early to really raise that alarm. For one, he could star without a ton of passing production as an all-purpose shotmaker in a multi-distributor offense. Second, he showed advanced passing reads as a prep star, and he might just need better health and superior scoring help around him to get back into that bag.

After three straight seasons with 64-plus losses, the Wizards are putting their losing ways behind them. Washington has organically grown a compelling young core and then supplemented it with established stars (Trae Young, Anthony Davis) and the No. 1 pick in a highly celebrated draft (AJ Dybantsa).
The Wizards even brought back Khris Middleton and turned their attention toward DeMar DeRozan after a failed courtship of Russell Westbrook.

Clearly, Washington thinks it is ready to turn the corner. A bit of brake-pumping feels warranted. Young is a one-way contributor, Davis can't stay on the court (and isn't a lock to stick around) and this young nucleus has won nothing at this level.
The future is bright—there's no denying that—but Washington may not be out of the woods just yet.

articles.title: Rose the Glitter-Breathing Dragon Revealed as New Mascot for WNBA's Portland Fire in Video, Photos
articles.summary: The Portland Fire unveiled their new mascot during Sunday's 105-100 loss to the Washington Mystics.
articles.body:
The Portland Fire unveiled their new mascot during Sunday's 105-100 loss to the Washington Mystics.

The organization hyped up the reveal by building a fake crater outside of Moda Center:

The otherworldly being that arrived on earth was Rose, the Glitter-Breathing Dragon:

"As the Fire returned to the court in 2026, Rose represents the Fire's spirit and relationship with Portland: passionate, unapologetic, and radiant," said Kimberly Veale, the Fire's senior vice president of marketing and communications. "She's a living modern force, embodying the vibe and self-assurance of a true Portland individualist that inspires us to truly flourish. As we get to know her, it's clear that she's got a little edge, a lot of personality, and after two decades waiting for her team to return, plenty of catching up to do."

Rose was unable to bring Portland any luck Sunday, and the Fire are on the brink of being eliminated from playoff contention. The game was a fabulous occasion nonetheless.

articles.title: Kobe Celebrated by Vanessa Bryant, Jeanie Buss on 'Mamba Day' and Birthday of Lakers Legend
articles.summary: Los Angeles Lakers team governor Jeanie Buss and the team honored franchise legend Kobe Bryant on what has been popularly dubbed "Mamba Day."
articles.body:
Los Angeles Lakers team governor Jeanie Buss and the team honored franchise legend Kobe Bryant on what has been popularly dubbed "Mamba Day."

Fans have come to celebrate Aug. 24 because it aligns with the jersey numbers Bryant wore in Los Angeles:

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

His birthday coincidentally fell a day earlier on the calendar. Vanessa Bryant took some time on Sunday to celebrate what would've been his 48th birthday:

Bryant was a five-time NBA champion, an 18-time All-Star and the 2007-08 MVP during his 20-year run in Southern California. He's the Lakers' all-time leader in games played, points and steals, and he ranks in the top five in rebounds and assists.

The organization has seen a number of Hall of Famers walk through the door, yet no Lakers player seemingly built a stronger relationship with the fanbase than Bryant.

Both of his jerseys are hanging in the rafters of Crypto.com Arena, and a statue in his likeness was unveiled outside of the venue in February 2024.

articles.title: DeWanna Bonner Lands Mercury Contract Buyout, Top Landing Spots for WNBA Star Amid Playoff Race
articles.summary: The Phoenix Mercury announced Monday that they bought out six-time All-Star DeWanna Bonner.
articles.body:
The Phoenix Mercury announced Monday that they bought out six-time All-Star DeWanna Bonner.

General manager Nick U'Ren said the move "gives her the opportunity to chase a title in what could be her final postseason" as the Mercury have already been eliminated from playoff contention.

Bonner's agent Mike Cound praised the Mercury after the move.

"They were great," Cound told Kareem Copeland of ESPN. "Many teams in the league wouldn't consider this, but this is a special circumstance and Phoenix is a very player-friendly organization. She's really appreciative of them."

Bonner averaged 10.6 points and 6.1 rebounds in 38 games with the team.

Any move to a contender will be complicated by the WNBA's hard salary cap and 12-player roster maximum. In terms of team needs and looking at the standings, the Las Vegas Aces, Dallas Wings and Washington Mystics all make sense.

The reigning WNBA champions are third in the league and now have a void in the frontcourt with NaLyssa Smith suffering a knee injury in in Sunday's 88-78 win over the Toronto Tempo.

Chalk it up to pure coincidence or fate, but Las Vegas could've seen one of its starters go down for the season and a prospective replacement emerge all within the space of 24 hours.

The Mystics and Wings are in similar positions in that they have emergent squads another year or two from seriously contending for a title.

In the case of Washington, Bonner would provide invaluable experience. Betnijah Laney-Hamilton is the only player on the active roster older than 27. That the Mystics are a playoff team while relying on so much youth is an achievement on its own.

Dallas has taken a big step forward in Paige Bueckers' second season.

The Wings showed ambition by poaching Jessica Shepard and co-Defensive Player of the Year Alanna Smith from the Minnesota Lynx. Shepard has exceeded expectations by making her first All-Star team, but Smith has seriously regressed. Bonner might make up some of the difference.

The Atlanta Dream could be in the mix, too.

From Bonner's perspective, they'd be more attractive than Dallas or Washington, and they've seen two key contributors in their frontcourt struggle to match their 2025 production. Naz Hillmon isn't the three-point threat she was en route to being Sixth Player of the Year, and Brionna Jones hasn't recaptured her All-Star form after suffering a torn meniscus while playing overseas.

Bonner turned 39 a few days ago and she's clearly no longer at her peak. She's still playing at a level that will make her useful for a top-eight team in the WNBA.

articles.title: Watch JJJ Get Pranked by Jazz HC, Keyonte George in Funny Video During Finland Trip with Markkanen
articles.summary: Members of the Utah Jazz weren't about to go to Finland and not have some fun.
articles.body:
Members of the Utah Jazz weren't about to go to Finland and not have some fun.

Head coach Will Hardy and guard Keyonte George pranked Jaren Jackson Jr. during the trip by pretending a room was sound proof and encouraging him to scream while in it. Naturally, Jackson can be heard screaming, which was quite amusing for the pranksters:

The trio was in Finland to visit teammate Lauri Markkanen, who is from the country.

It seems as if Hardy and George made sure there was plenty of team bonding along the way, even if it came at Jackson's expense.

articles.title: 'Sugar to S--t,' LaVar Ball Trolls Hornets After LaMelo Was Traded to Wolves
articles.summary: The Charlotte Hornets opted to trade star point guard LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves this offseason, and LaVar Ball thinks his son's former team is in for a rough year.
articles.body:
The Charlotte Hornets opted to trade star point guard LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves this offseason, and LaVar Ball thinks his son's former team is in for a rough year.

LaVar said on Ultimate Dads Unplugged that he thinks the Hornets are going to "go from sugar to s--t real quick," but he's ultimately happy with the move because it gives LaMelo the chance to compete for a title.

"When he was on there, I told him two things. I said, 'Yo, you ain't never win no championship just with Melo by himself. What you must do is get is get his two brothers or trade him.' And they traded him the next day, so it's all good," he said (12:10 mark).

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

Jayson Tatum's dad blunt about Celtics roster

The Hornets traded LaMelo to Minnesota in return for Naz Reid, an unprotected first-round pick in 2033, three first-round pick swaps in 2028, 2029 and 2030, and three second-round picks in 2029, 2032 and 2033.

The move perhaps indicated that Charlotte is shifting towards building around Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel.

LaMelo is coming off a season in which he put up 20.1 points, 7.1 assists and 4.8 rebounds per game, marking one of the best years of his career. The Hornets were close to sneaking into the playoffs for the first time in years, but they still decided it was time to move on.

Whether they made the right call to trade LaMelo remains to be seen, but LaVar believes they'll regret it.

articles.title: Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White Are Not Eligible for the WNBA Draft, AP Source Says
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible for the WNBA draft, a person familiar with the decision said Monday.
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible for the WNBA draft, a person familiar with the decision said Monday.

The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the situation. The person did not elaborate on the reasons for declaring the two men ineligible.

Freedom and White have declared their intention to enter next year's draft, but the WNBA has not publicly addressed their eligibility.

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. When they announced their intention to enter the draft, Freedom and White said they identified as women.

The 6-foot-10, 250-pound Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA. White played in three NBA games.

Freedom was ejected from Sunday night's Indiana-Chicago game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Freedom's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Freedom, 34, as she approached him. A standing Freedom held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.

Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.

"I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!" Freedom wrote on social media Sunday night. "Let that sink in, AMERICA!"

Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.

Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls' and women's sports, and since then the league has been embroiled in debates about transgender participation. Freedom joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. When they announced their intention to enter the draft, Freedom and White said they identified as women.
The 6-foot-10, 250-pound Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA. White played in three NBA games.
Freedom was ejected from Sunday night's Indiana-Chicago game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.
Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Freedom's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Freedom, 34, as she approached him. A standing Freedom held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.

Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.
He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.
"I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!" Freedom wrote on social media Sunday night. "Let that sink in, AMERICA!"
Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.

Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls' and women's sports, and since then the league has been embroiled in debates about transgender participation. Freedom joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.

articles.title: Angel Reese Breaks 2 WNBA Records, Final Box Score Stats, Highlights as Dream Beat Brink, Sparks
articles.summary: Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream remain red hot after she broke two WNBA records to lead the team to a 78-71 win over the Los Angeles Sparks.
articles.body:
Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream remain red hot after she broke two WNBA records to lead the team to a 78-71 win over the Los Angeles Sparks.

The Dream, who were favored by 10.5 points at FanDuel, faced a much bigger test than their last matchup with the Sparks on Aug. 20 that they won by 36 points.

Reese helped them hold off Los Angeles by recording a WNBA single-game record 26 rebounds. She also set a single-season record in total rebounds during the game at 458 with six games remaining in the regular season.

Reese broke the single-season record for total rebounds with 6:17 remaining in the fourth quarter when she grabbed an offensive board off a missed layup. She passed A'ja Wilson's record of 451 set in 2024.

The 26 total rebounds in a game broke the record that had stood for 23 years. Chamique Holdsclaw had held the single-game mark of 24 rebounds since May 23, 2003.

"That's a talent," Dream guard Allisha Gray said of Reese after the win. "I'm just in awe watching her rebound."

This marks the second consecutive game against the Sparks in which Reese has made WNBA history. Her previous outing four days ago saw her become the first player to have at least 20 points, 10 rebounds, five assists and three steals without missing a shot.

Reese has led the Dream (25-13) to four consecutive wins and six victories in their last seven games. They remain in the No. 4 spot in the playoff race, just one-half game behind the Las Vegas Aces for the three seed.

Atlanta is off until Friday when it will host the Connecticut Sun before the WNBA takes a three-week break for the FIBA World Cup.

articles.title: Warriors Sign Former Mavs Guard Brandon Williams to Contract, Updated Roster, Salary Cap
articles.summary: The Golden State Warriors have signed free agent guard Brandon Williams to a one-year, $2.6 million contract, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors have signed free agent guard Brandon Williams to a one-year, $2.6 million contract, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

Here's a look at the team's current active roster and salary cap situation.

Heat still have 2 rosters spot left after signing Klay

Jayson Tatum's dad blunt about Celtics roster

PG : Stephen Curry, De'Anthony Melton, Brandon Williams, LJ Cryer

SG : Brandin Podziemski, Gary Payton II, Will Richard

C : Kristaps Porzingis, Al Horford, Charles Bassey

Per Spotrac , the Warriors had roughly $249.4 million allocated toward the 2026-27 salary cap before landing Williams, which will now put them at about $252 million. They are now below the second apron threshold by about $2.6 million.

Williams, 26, is a 6'1" guard who has played four NBA seasons. He played 24 games (16 starts) with the 2021-22 Portland Trail Blazers but didn't see any NBA action in 2022-23. That year, Williams played for the G League's College Park Skyhawks.

Williams has also suited up for the G League's Westchester Knicks (2021-22) and Osceola Magic (2023).

In Dec. 2023, Williams signed a two-way deal with the Dallas Mavericks. He's played 116 games over three seasons with the Mavs, including 66 in 2023-24 (15 starts).

He averaged 13.0 points, 3.9 assists and 2.9 rebounds over 22.2 minutes per game last season.

Earlier in August, NBA insider Marc Stein reported that the Warriors were interested in Williams and forward Georges Niang for their remaining open roster spots.

In the end, Golden State added Williams to the roster as the team hopes to make the playoffs after an injury-plagued 2025-26 season ended one game short of that feat after a loss to the Phoenix Suns in the Western Conference play-in tournament.

articles.title: LeBron James partners with PGA Tour to host new golf event in Akron, Ohio
articles.summary: LeBron James is making sure golf remains an important sport in his hometown.
articles.body:
LeBron James, the newest star for the Philadelphia 76ers, gained plenty of attention when he launched a YouTube channel focused on golf in August. If that wasn't enough of an indication, James is apparently far more into the sport than expected. He continued to put his love of the sport on display Tuesday, when it was announced James had teamed up with the PGA Tour to bring a new golf event to his hometown.

The LeBron James Family Foundation Invitational will be played in Akron, Ohio, in 2027, per ESPN. The inaugural event will occur July 6 through July 7 and be played at the South Course at Firestone Country Club.

The event will be focused on helping kids see the benefits of golf. The LeBron James Family Foundation Invitational will feature " amateurs and pros from the tour's Pathway to Progression Pro-Bound Five program," per ESPN.

In a statement, James talked about the ways the sport can open doors and build relationships .

"Golf has become a passion of mine, and I've seen firsthand how the game can open doors, build relationships and create opportunities that many kids don't even know exist," James said in a statement. "This partnership with the PGA Tour gives my foundation a chance to introduce my I Promise students and more people to the game at a young age, support talented athletes chasing their dreams, and continue investing in the city of Akron that means everything to me."

The Pathway to Progression Pro-Bound Five program was established in 2024 to provide "opportunities for talented golfers from underrepresented communities to strengthen the pipeline of future professional talent and its audience," per the PGA's website. The program also has a collegiate tier, in which the top-five ranked players gain membership access to the Advocates Professional Golf Association (APGA) Tour.

James' event will connect students from his foundation's I Promise program with pro golfers who came up through the Pathway to Progression program. It will also include off-course mentorship programs between students and players.

Firestone Country Club has played host to many pro golfing events over the years. Most recently, the Senior Players Championship was held at the course from 2019 through 2026. But in May, it was announced that the event would be moved to California in 2027, paving the way for James to host a new event in his hometown.

articles.title: ‘Outrageous’: Analyst furious after Sophie Cunningham passed over for ‘hottest player’ in WNBA
articles.summary: Indiana Fever reserve guard Sophie Cunningham endeared herself to a lot of people when she advocated against the participation of transgender athletes in wom...
articles.body:
Indiana Fever reserve guard Sophie Cunningham endeared herself to a lot of people when she advocated against the participation of transgender athletes in women's sports in a July 21 ESPN profile.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" she said in the feature. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Unfortunately, a viral TikTok from Sportico exposed that many of these "new fans" don't actually care about the basketball being played in the league and instead view the WNBA as a vehicle to advance their own political agendas.

Nevertheless, people and outlets continue to back Cunningham for reasons that have nothing to do with basketball. On Tuesday, Outkick's Bobby Burack was upset with The Daily W, a WNBA podcast, for ranking Sophie Cunningham behind Seattle Storm rookie Awa Fam and Sky guard DiJonai Carrington on its list of the "hottest players" in the league.

"Okay, this is nuts," Burack posted on X.

"A WNBA podcast discussed the 'hottest player in the league' (based on looks) and picked DiJonai Carrington and Awa Fam. They didn't even mention Sophie Cunningham or Cam Brink. Outrageous."

If Burack was a true Cunningham fan, he'd recognize that she wants the focus to be on the basketball being played in the league, and likely doesn't care at all about rankings such as these. However, his take is far from surprising. His colleague at Outkick, Dan Dakich, called Cunningham's superstar teammate Caitlin Clark "kinda cute."

Hopefully, with football season right around the corner, people who have no real interest in the WNBA will return their focus to sports they're actually interested in so that real fans can enjoy the league without the outside noise.

articles.title: Enes Kanter Freedom not welcome back at Sky home games after ejection, confrontation: 'He made himself into a threat'
articles.summary: Enes Kanter Freedom was thrown out of the Sky's loss to the Fever on Sunday night after a confrontation with Natasha Cloud.
articles.body:
Enes Kanter Freedom is not welcome back at Wintrust Arena anytime soon.

Chicago Sky owner Michael Alter spoke out about the recent incident involving Kanter Freedom and star Natasha Cloud on Tuesday. Kanter Freedom, Alter said, is not allowed back at Wintrust Arena until "he's able to prove to us that he's able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat."

"It was pretty clear to us that his purpose of coming here was trying to be as provocative and just see how much attention he could get," Alter said, via Front Office Sports' Colin Salao .

The incident occurred during the third quarter of the Sky's loss to the Indiana Fever on Sunday . After making a layup, Cloud turned and erupted at Kanter Freedom, who was sitting along the baseline. She had to be held back by several teammates. Kanter Freedom, who started taking steps toward the court, was then stopped and walked out of the arena by security. He was seen arguing with security and police before actually leaving the arena, too.

Alter said Tuesday that, after speaking to several people who were seated next to Kanter Freedom at the game, the dialogue started with him.

"He began to chirp with her sometime in the third quarter," Alter said. "I would characterize it as trash talking, nothing personal. Basketball-related, but enough to get her attention and to engage with her, and in my opinion, to try to provoke her."

Kanter Freedom spent 11 seasons in the NBA from 2011-2022. He legally changed his last name to "Freedom" in 2021 after becoming a United States citizen.

Kanter Freedom has thrown himself into the transgender athlete discussions that have surrounded the league in recent weeks, which started largely after Fever guard Sophie Cunningham spoke out about the topic in an ESPN feature. Cunningham supported barring transgender athletes from women's sports, which has led to anti-trans protests outside of Fever away games, among other things.

Kanter Freedom was wearing a black T-shirt with a definition for the word "woman" on it on Sunday night. He's even claimed that he is now a "WNBA prospect" on social media, and claimed after Sunday's incident that he was kicked out "for supporting women."

There are no transgender players in the WNBA or preparing to enter the WNBA, and there are no legitimate eligibility matters facing the league, either. The CBA states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." Kanter and former NBA player Royce White are not eligible to play in the league, either, despite declaring themselves eligible and saying they identified as women .

"He portrays as this victimless person who did nothing, said nothing," Alter said. "Just [someone] wearing a T-shirt … We have five different security authorities that all agreed very quickly to throw him out because he made himself into a threat."

Alter said he only learned that Kanter was coming to the game a few hours before tip on Sunday, and that his "one regret" from this incident was not telling his players about the situation. He said they didn't know where Kanter was going to be sitting ahead of time.

The Sky hold a 15-23 record entering Tuesday's contest with the Connecticut Sun . They have already been eliminated from playoff contention.

The WNBA has not announced any plans to ban or prevent Kanter Freedom from attending games elsewhere. But for now, at least Sky home games appear to be off-limits.

articles.title: Cavs' Donovan Mitchell Reacts to Wife Coco Jones Landing 'Hilary' Role in 'Bel-Air' Spin-Off
articles.summary: Cleveland Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell has his eyes on a new upcoming show.
articles.body:
Cleveland Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell has his eyes on a new upcoming show.

Which isn't exactly surprising considering his wife, Coco Jones, is going to star in it:

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

articles.title: Sky Owner Says Enes Kanter Freedom is Banned From Home Games, Calling Him 'A Potential Threat'
articles.summary: CHICAGO (AP) — The Chicago Sky have banned Enes Kanter Freedom from their home games after the former NBA center was ejected from Sunday's loss to the Indiana Fever.
articles.body:
CHICAGO (AP) — The Chicago Sky have banned Enes Kanter Freedom from their home games after the former NBA center was ejected from Sunday's loss to the Indiana Fever.

Owner Michael Alter made the announcement in a rare news conference on Tuesday. Alter told reporters Freedom is not allowed inside of Wintrust Arena for Sky games "unless sometime in the future, he's able to prove to us that he's able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat."

The 6-foot-10, 250-pound Freedom was removed from Sunday's game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Enes Kanter Freedom Ejected from WNBA Game

Source: Freedom, White Not Eligible for WNBA Draft (AP)

Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Freedom's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Freedom, 34, as she approached him. A standing Freedom held his arms out and stepped onto the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.

"It was pretty clear to us that his purpose of coming here was trying to be provocative and see how much attention he could get," Alter told reporters from the Chicago Sun-Times and other media outlets.

Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing the arena.

"I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!" Freedom wrote on social media. "Let that sink in, AMERICA!"

Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women. But a person familiar with the decision told the AP on Monday that they are not eligible. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the situation.

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

articles.title: Watch Penny Hardaway's motivational speech to Memphis football team
articles.summary: Penny Hardaway spoke to the Memphis football team ahead of the 2026 season. Here's what he told them about what it means to play for the Tigers.
articles.body:
Memphis football coach Charles Huff said at his news conference on Aug. 25 that motivational speeches don't mean much once the game actually starts.

But he also said that after Memphis basketball coach Penny Hardaway delivered an impassioned one to the football team about what it means to play at Memphis.

"We carry the city," Hardaway said in a speech that was posted on social media. "We win, it makes our whole entire city better. The people are more happy. The crime goes down, it's already been documented. So when you have that on you, it should mean something. Whether you care about the city of Memphis or not, it should mean something to you. That pride should mean something."

Hardaway would know. He's a Memphis native who played for the Tigers before going to the NBA, eventually returning to Memphis as head basketball coach. He and Huff have built a strong relationship in the time since Huff was hired in December. He already has visited a football practice and said he plans to be around more during the season.

Memphis football has an entirely new coaching staff and a roster made up mostly of transfers. Huff has talked throughout the offseason about using Hardaway to explain to those players what it means to play for the Tigers.

"I was the No. 1 player in the high school rankings," Hardaway said. "I could've went anywhere in the country. I chose to stay home. I didn't choose to stay home because I was a home guy. I chose it because of how the fans made me feel for sure. And that's the same thing that y'all are going to get. You perform at a high level in this city, they treat you like royalty. The reason why is because this thing goes deeper than just tickets to a game. The city will ride with you as long as you're doing what you're supposed to do."

The football team kicks off its season at UNLV on Aug. 29 (9 p.m. CT, FOX). Memphis basketball's season begins on Nov. 2 against Iowa State in Sioux Falls, South Dakota.

In his speech to the team, Hardaway talked about what it means to play for Tigers fans.

"Y'all have to understand: The days you don't want to get up, the days you don't want to do the extra reps, you've got to push all that to the side because that's nothing compared to what these people have to go through every day," he said. "And spend their money to come and watch y'all play."

Reach sports writer Jonah Dylan at jonah.dylan@commercialappeal.com or on X @thejonahdylan .

articles.title: Entering contract year, Cason Wallace shows off scoring bag in offseason run
articles.summary: Entering contract year, Cason Wallace shows off scoring bag in offseason run.
articles.body:
In the final week of August, we're in the dog days of summer. Very little is going on in the NBA world. Most of the offseason homework is done and teams are awaiting training camps to start. Right now, everybody is bored out of their mind. But right around the corner, we're about to see the yearly marathon restart.

The Oklahoma City Thunder enter the 2026-27 season as a co-title favorite — alongside the San Antonio Spurs . Even with their cost-cutting moves this offseason, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander , Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren should be enough to keep you in the title hunt.

But with Lu Dort and others out the door, Cason Wallace could be in line for a massive promotion. The 22-year-old will likely become a full-time starter this upcoming season. He'll no longer have to call himself the unofficial sixth starter as he has over the first three seasons of his rich basketball career. He'll also get more opportunities to grow on offense.

With a vacuum of possessions and shot attempts up for grabs, Wallace should see an uptick in offensive production. No longer will he have to settle for catch-and-shoot looks with the occasional downhill drive. Now, OKC's success could depend on his development on that side of the floor. It looks like he's taking it seriously this summer.

Wallace showed off his ball-handling creativity in a recent open gym run. He also showed he can pull up from deep outside. In a social media video that highlighted his best plays, he showed some finesse around his driving game as he kissed the ball off the glass for a layup. Everything is set up for him to be a double-digit scorer for the first time in his career this upcoming season. It's now about running away with that opportunity.

These summer months are when NBA players usually make the most strides in their respective games. The downtime allows them to work on their craft undisturbed. It'll be interesting to see how Wallace looks as he's about to enter his fourth NBA season already.

articles.title: Timberwolves’ LaMelo Ball hires driver following reckless driving incidents in Charlotte, brother Lonzo says
articles.summary: Lonzo Ball revealed that LaMelo Ball has a driver to help with his many road situations after buying $1 million cars and finding ways to damage them.
articles.body: LaMelo Ball’s extensive car collection has drawn attention since his rise to basketball stardom. But the Minnesota Timberwolves guard has now decided to employ a personal driver to help him get around his new NBA home, according to his older brother, Lonzo Ball. During a recent edition of the "Curious Mike" podcast, Lonzo Ball pointed to his younger brother while discussing which member of the Ball family spends the most money with Brooklyn Nets forward Michael Porter Jr. "Who in your family out of y'all three spends the most [money]," Porter asked. "The one who has the most, LaMelo," Lonzo replied. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM "[He's] got 10 cars," Lonzo continued. Having a driver could mean the 25-year-old spends less time behind the wheel and, in turn, has fewer opportunities to be involved in an accident. Lonzo also suggested LaMelo could benefit from choosing vehicles outside the exotic-car category, rather than Lamborghinis and similar high-performance models he has owned in the past. LAMELO BALL'S CUSTOM HUMMER LOSES WHEEL IN CHARLOTTE CRASH DURING ALL-STAR BREAK "He'll buy a $1 million car and then just immediately f–k it up, I've never understood [that]," Lonzo added in reference to his sibling's habits when it comes to vehicles. "You just bought that? And then you ripped it up? You could've just got a beater," the former Los Angeles Lakers guard noted. Lonzo then addressed the perception surrounding the frequency of LaMelo’s road incidents, saying his younger brother "doesn’t get into accidents, but he has a lot of situations on the road." The Lakers selected Lonzo Ball with the second overall pick in the 2017 NBA Draft. He later played for the New Orleans Pelicans and Chicago Bulls before joining the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2025. The Cavaliers traded him to the Utah Jazz in February 2026, but the Jazz subsequently waived him before he appeared in a game for the team. Lonzo's NBA career has been marked by injuries. After appearing in 35 games during the 2021-22 season, he spent more than two calendar years sidelined. "It was like a 1,000 and something days," Ball said, reflecting on the length of his absence. He added that he has come to terms with the possibility that he may not return to the same level he once reached as an athlete. "I came at peace with that when I got hurt the first time. Every time you get hurt it kind of sets you back," Ball told Porter. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Hornets selected LaMelo with the third overall pick in the 2020 NBA Draft. Charlotte traded the two-time All-Star guard and his teammates Josh Green to the Timberwolves in June for Naz Reid and multiple draft picks.
